candidates.title: When Answering Is Administering: Permission Replies That Rewrite Coding-Agent Policy
candidates.author: Zeming Fei, Hongming Fei, Jingwen Chen, Xiaoyang Wang, Prosanta Gope, Biplab Sikdar, Ying Zhang
candidates.organization: University of Technology Sydney, National University of Singapore, UNSW, University of Sheffield
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-24 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 25 cs.CR listing)
candidates.what_changed: Shows that in Claude Code a party allowed only to answer permission prompts (plugin hook, prompt handler, SDK host, remote front end incl. the vendor's own Remote Control) can attach policy updates that delete the operator's deny rules; still works on Claude Code 2.1.327.
candidates.mechanism: Claude Code lets an answer carry policy updates (add/remove/replace rules, setMode, addDirectories) that the runtime persists to settings files. Its filter (read from the binary, builds 2.1.231-2.1.325) only checks updates that add or replace allow rules, so removeRules on deny passes. Deletion is logged identically to a local operator edit.
candidates.evidence_quality: Strong: attack demonstrated on all four answer routes, scripted and live models (claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-opus-5-5) with and without strict sandbox; formal tight bounds; predictions across 13 permission designs in 10 agent systems incl. 4 pre-registered (Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode, Goose); repair implemented on patched local binaries; 20,000 random runs.
candidates.relevance: Very high: directly actionable for anyone delegating permission prompts in Claude Code or similar agents.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Advances Edition 4 'rules file vs gate' (Markdown Is Not a Firewall): here the gate's own policy is rewritable through the approval channel. New material.
candidates.summary: Operators write allow/deny rules (e.g. deny Read(./.env)); prompts can be answered by four non-terminal routes: plugin hooks, a prompt handler for unattended sessions, SDK embedding apps, and remote front ends via a bridge. An answer may carry policy updates; intended for 'always allow'. Claude Code documents an answer cannot override a matching deny rule, and the vendor has fixed that per-decision check three times, but the update path is unchecked except for allow add/replace. Attack: remote approval service with no file access approves an unrelated 'touch' and attaches an update deleting the .env deny rule; agent then reads secrets in that session and later ones, even under strict sandbox; one more update lets a later command send them out. Survey of 70 permission relays: 5 forward rule updates including deny removals (about 7%, incl. Anthropic's Remote Control, whose schema accepts all update types; the open-source ones total >40,000 GitHub stars), 25 offer a choice among proposed updates, 37 send decision only, 3 undeterminable. Managed-tier rules held (no route writes the managed tier). Theory: a runtime without authorship records can safely accept only updates that keep every currently denied call denied; with authorship it can let each party remove only its own restrictions; both bounds tight; exact deletion checking is coNP-hard with mixed wildcards. Repair: a validator at the shared update step that drops deletions/replacements of deny rules; it kept restrictions in all attack runs while honest updates still applied; only 2 of 2,227 marketplace plugins (about 0.1%) send updates it would change. Interim mitigation (paper): keep deny rules in the managed tier or in a settings file passed on the command line, which no update reaches; restrict sandbox network to hosts managed settings allow. Disclosure status to vendor: UNVERIFIED (not stated in what I read).

candidates.title: LLM Agent Authorization Across Context Compaction
candidates.author: Zeming Fei, Hongming Fei, Yi Xu, Xiaoyang Wang, Ying Zhang
candidates.organization: University of Technology Sydney, National University of Singapore, UNSW
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-24 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 25 cs.CR listing)
candidates.what_changed: Finds that Claude Code and Codex insert the compaction summary as a user message at all 1,108 automatic compactions observed, so request-derived authorizers (e.g. Progent) start granting permissions based on what the compactor wrote, including attacker data.
candidates.mechanism: Authorizers read the 'request slot' (latest user message). After compaction the model-written summary occupies it; injected data that looks like legitimate data (a payee account in a notice) is quoted as if the user said it. Fix: authenticate user text on arrival and carry it verbatim across compaction to the authorizer, while the agent still reads the summary.
candidates.evidence_quality: Strong: measurements on deployed Claude Code and Codex, compaction prompts of 11 harnesses, frontier compactors, proof of tight bound, AgentDojo end-to-end and 8 adaptive attacks.
candidates.relevance: High: anyone building per-request permission policies or LLM reviewers for long-running agents.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Related to Edition 4 gate theme and Edition 3 context engineering (compaction); new angle (compaction as a security boundary).
candidates.summary: Eight more harnesses' compaction code also places the summary as a user message: Gemini CLI, OpenHands, Cline, Goose, Aider, Qwen Code, Kimi CLI, LangChain. With a small compactor, injections Progent blocks before compaction succeed after it about as often as on an undefended agent. Rent-payment case: when an attacker's notice states another account as plain data and the user asks to pay rent, the policy derived from a frontier compactor's summary admits the attacker account in 91% of cases vs 0% when derived from the user's own words. Frontier compactors mark injected instructions but rarely injected data (which has a legitimate twin). Theorem: an authorizer that can't see who wrote which bytes can't treat a forged record differently from the legitimate one by more than they are distinguishable; bound tight. Fix gate: authorizer credits only authenticated user text carried verbatim; attacker can block the policy but not shape it. In 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes rerun with the fix, no attacker action completes; withstands 8 adaptive attacks including records replayed via files the agent can write, which pass the authors' implementation of the simpler filter OpenAI deployed in Codex. Key line: 'What a compactor keeps, and how it marks it, is a security parameter.'

candidates.title: ParseGap: Testing What Coding Agents Authorize and What Shells Execute
candidates.author: Jieyu Li
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-22 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.CR listing)
candidates.what_changed: Differential testing of eight production coding agents' shell-command gates vs GNU Bash 5.2 finds 17 root causes where an approved command does something the policy forbids; proposes ShellPlan, which compiles commands once and execve's them without a shell.
candidates.mechanism: Gate parses the string with its own parser (shell-quote, tree-sitter-bash, Starlark prefix rules) then hands the raw string to /bin/bash; three divergence boundaries: parse (checker sees one command, shell runs two), utility (allowlisted read-only binaries with writing/exec arguments), confinement (an allow rule disables the OS sandbox).
candidates.evidence_quality: Strong: unmodified vendor checkers, isolated containers, 4,174 active attack cases across six suites, live trials with two models on all 8 CLIs, formal model; single author.
candidates.relevance: Very high: anyone allowlisting 'read-only' shell commands for agents.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Extends Edition 4 'only a gate decides' theme: shows gates themselves misread commands. New.
candidates.summary: Agents studied: Codex CLI 0.171.0, Gemini CLI 0.70.0, Qwen Code 0.28.3, Mistral Vibe 3.1.4, OpenCode, Cline, Continue, Roo Code (Claude Code not in set). Running example: read-only policy allowing uniq; 'uniq README.md /var/tmp/x' writes outside the workspace (uniq's second operand is an output file); 6 of 8 agents allow it. In Codex CLI read-only sandbox mode, matching a Starlark allow rule disables the bwrap+Landlock sandbox (policy-sandbox inversion, RC-14); under strace live sessions spawned zero bwrap processes and an allowlisted sed with an execute directive spawned /bin/sh to run a forbidden touch. Upstream tree-sitter-bash multi-line lexical defect hides a second command from Mistral Vibe and Gemini CLI (bytes redacted pending coordinated disclosure). Qwen Code: a user allow rule on an outer command silently upgrades a nested-substitution 'ask' to allow. Utility divergence: every checker allowed read-only binaries whose arguments write files or launch programs (9-47 of 55 cases; e.g. Continue 9/55, Mistral Vibe 20/55). Live trials: policy violations in all 16 agent-model pairs (14 under configured restrictions) with gpt-5.6-luna and deepseek-v4.1-flash. ShellPlan: compile a strict Bash subset into a typed plan, validate utility arguments against positive capability specs, validate git configs, dispatch via execve; 0/4,174 attacks admitted, 0/90 hits in a ten-model benchmark (62/90 unguarded), 1.28 ms median gate latency, 36/36 frontier standard-dev completion (74/100 overall), integrated live into unmodified Codex CLI.

candidates.title: Oops!... I Parsed It Again: Tool-Call Smuggling Against LLM Agents
candidates.author: Igor Santos-Grueiro, Daniel Romero-Ruiz
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-23 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.CR listing)
candidates.what_changed: Defines tool-call smuggling: the guard and executor parse the same JSON tool-call bytes differently (duplicate keys, case folding, escapes), so the guard approves one call, the executor runs another, and the audit log records the approved one.
candidates.mechanism: JSON leaves choices to each parser (which duplicate key wins, case-insensitive matching, NUL/escape handling, undeclared fields, JSON-in-string). Six vectors; differential harness over 17 pinned parser/validator configurations. Fix: parse once, keep only approved-schema fields, seal with call ID to the executor.
candidates.evidence_quality: Strong: differential harness, 4,693 deployed MCP schemas, end-to-end attacks on tau-bench and AgentDojo, ten models tested; cites prior real CVEs/GHSAs as isolated instances.
candidates.relevance: High: MCP gateway, guard and SDK builders; anyone whose audit log trusts the guard's view.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Same family as Edition 4 'Subverting Tool Arguments' (2611.27041) but a distinct mechanism (parser differential, not metadata poisoning).
candidates.summary: Example: tau-bench airline task; compromised gateway rewrites the call so reservation_id names another customer's reservation and Reservation_ID the user's; Go's default decoder (guard) ignores case and keeps the last match and approves the user's; an official MCP SDK (executor) keeps the exact name and cancels the other; log shows approved cancellation of the user's. Prior isolated reports: MCP Go SDK case-insensitive field matching (CVE-2026-27896), its replacement parser reading a key with trailing NUL as the key without it (GHSA-q382-vc8q-7jhj), Envoy AI Gateway logging ALLOWED for one call while backend ran another (GHSA-4gph-2hhr-5mwg). Findings: most pairs of 12 parsers and 5 validators disagree on some inputs; two official MCP SDKs accept different inputs (split on 21 of 22 inputs of one class); 558 of 4,693 deployed MCP schemas give different arguments or verdicts across components. Escaped file name passes a data-loss guard and becomes credentials.txt. Models (10 tested) don't write duplicate/disguised keys into the call itself but copy them verbatim into JSON text inside a string argument, which a Python guard and a Go executor read differently. A malicious server copying a legit tool's schema and adding one field (explained by a note) gets the model to fill it with user data unseen by the guard. Fix stops all 7,412 crafted inputs and every attack built.

candidates.title: SchemaCaps: When a Compatible Tool Update Silently Widens an AI Agent's Authority
candidates.author: Yulliwas Ameur, Samia Bouzefrane, Soumya Banerjee
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-23 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.AI listing)
candidates.what_changed: Shows that MCP tool input-schema changes that are 'backward compatible' often widen the authority of an already-approved tool, and none of 8 surveyed MCP clients/scanners re-approves on schema widening.
candidates.mechanism: Defines non-amplification over schema-visible coordinates (declared args, undeclared fields, effective values) and a re-binding rule decided by subschema inclusion; re-approval required when a new schema is not a subschema of the approved one.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate: Coq proof, 48 regression tests, pilot on 604 releases of 39 public MCP servers; double annotation; authors note their own reviewed rule version silently re-bound 27 amplifying changes (since fixed). HTML version not available (404); numbers are from the abstract only.
candidates.relevance: High for MCP client/gateway builders and teams pinning tool versions.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: New; complements tool-call smuggling and Edition 4 tool-argument poisoning.
candidates.summary: Of 8 surveyed MCP clients and scanners, none observed or documented to re-approve a tool whose input schema widens (two not determinable). Pilot: 604 releases of 39 public MCP servers; 412 of 580 compatible schema changes widen some coordinate, yet compatibility re-binds them silently. Adjudicated double annotation: at least 76 add or widen an authority-bearing argument (66 of the 84 a name-based labeller flags, plus 10 it misses). Approval cost on existing tools: the rule asks 645 re-approvals vs 1,197 for pinning the input schema (2,004 if descriptions also pinned) and 617 for plain compatibility. Limitation: behaviour change behind an identical schema is out of reach.

candidates.title: Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents? An Empirical Study of Hidden AI-Directed Text on GitHub
candidates.author: Gabi Nakibly, Zvika Babo
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-21 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.CR listing)
candidates.what_changed: First large-scale census of hidden AI-directed text on GitHub: 2,281 validated findings in 142.7M issues/PRs/comments (16 per million) plus 107 READMEs; attacks rare but aimed at maintainers' own triage/review/CI agents; first-party hidden 'orchestration' markers dominate and are forgeable.
candidates.mechanism: Concealment-based detection (HTML comments never rendered on GitHub but present in raw text agents receive; also Unicode tag chars, CSS hiding in READMEs), bot-marker noise filter, two-stage LLM classification, template provenance check against each repo's issue/PR template history, manual review.
candidates.evidence_quality: Strong: very large corpus, manual review of all findings, released tool and data; offline replay of 43 attacks against 5 models.
candidates.relevance: Very high: anyone running agents on issues/PRs; cheap mitigation (strip HTML comments) shown effective.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 2 covered sandboxing; Edition 4 rules-file security. This is new field measurement.
candidates.summary: Example: issue #28575 of google-gemini/gemini-cli (July 2026) looks like an ordinary bug report but contains an HTML comment beginning 'SYSTEM MAINTENANCE OVERRIDE - DO NOT REMOVE'. Four uses: attacks on others' agents, defensive text restricting agents, content override steering what agents write, first-party orchestration via hidden markers. Findings across 435 repositories; rate comparable to about 13 per million pages on the open web. Attacks about 1 in 3.3 million items. Orchestration is two thirds of findings in issues/PRs/comments, grew fivefold in four months, and forms a control channel anyone who can comment can imitate, including 47 markers in 10 projects that record approvals or bypassed checks. Without the template check, 60% of classifier-confirmed findings would be misattributed (template guidance). Replay of 43 attacks against five models: one small fast model complies in 19% of cases; none once HTML comments are stripped. Detection tool and all findings released.

candidates.title: Carried-Over and Agent-Native Threats in the Supply Chain of LLM Agent Skills
candidates.author: Kaixuan Li, Wenbo Guo, Sen Chen, Yang Liu
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-23 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.CR listing)
candidates.what_changed: Registry-scale study of all 48,682 skills on ClawHub: half of skills with resolvable dependencies pin a version with a known CVE (78.3% born vulnerable), but few CVEs are reachable; first-party code flaws are the real risk; injected payloads mostly run in the agent's own shell before the skill does.
candidates.mechanism: Static analysis screen of all skills, manual review of 3,428 flagged cases, sandbox reachability testing, live LLM agent under indirect prompt injection.
candidates.evidence_quality: Strong: full-registry census plus manual review and dynamic confirmation.
candidates.relevance: High: teams adopting third-party skills or running skill registries.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: New (Edition 2 brief covered stale skills, not supply chain).
candidates.summary: Four risks: dependencies and first-party code (carried over), install instructions and credentials printed to stdout (agent-native). 49.6% of skills with resolvable dependencies depend on a version with a known CVE; unlike npm packages that mostly become vulnerable after release, 78.3% are vulnerable at publication. Agent input reaches the vulnerable function in only 3.0% of affected skills, whereas 21 of 22 sampled first-party flaws are exploited end to end in the sandbox. A live agent executes the injected payload in 48.5% of sampled flagged skills, but almost always in its own shell before the skill runs; payload reaches a flaw in the skill itself in only 5.0%. Recommendations: registries should prioritize first-party flaws over dependency alerts, and agent runtimes should not pass skill arguments through a shell. Related same-window paper: 'Demystifying Detectors Guarding Agent Skill Hubs' (arXiv 2611.30913): best hub-adopted detector (skill-scanner with Qwen3.6) misses 4.9% of malicious skills and flags 17.8% of benign; prompt refinement of skill-vetter improves F1 by up to 22.7 points.

candidates.title: Ads for Agents: Measuring Ad-Serving MCP Servers
candidates.author: Shahrooz Pouryousef, Sohini Chakraborty, Ali Montazer, Muoi Tran
candidates.organization: Chalmers University of Technology / University of Gothenburg, Stockholm University
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-21 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.CR listing)
candidates.what_changed: First measurement of MCP servers that inject paid ads into tool results: rare (0.57% of 101,363 open endpoints) but mostly operator-inserted, rarely labeled (9.3%), with hidden link destinations; proposes a per-item ad annotation in MCP results.
candidates.mechanism: Discovered servers via ad networks, package registries, certificate logs, hostnames, MCP directories and GitHub configs; read-only queries; inspected ad links.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate-strong: broad discovery, read-only probing.
candidates.relevance: Medium-high: MCP consumers deciding which servers to trust; spec-level proposal.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: New.
candidates.summary: Ads appear on 0.57% of 101,363 open MCP endpoints and 0.04% of 122,656 local MCP packages. 173 ad networks target agents, yet operators insert ads themselves on about half of the 226 ad-returning servers; nearly all ad-serving packages carry the operator's own affiliate ID. Ads adapt to the query's topic and intent but disclosure stays fixed within each tool. Only 9.3% carry an explicit sponsored label; most links hide destinations. The model decides whether ads and disclosures reach the user. Proposal: per-item ad annotation in MCP results that clients can show independently of the model's answer.

candidates.title: The Effect of Security-Focused Prompts on Reported Findings: A Controlled Experiment on 400 AI-Generated Web Applications
candidates.author: Darko Androcec
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-20 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.AI listing)
candidates.what_changed: Controlled experiment: appending a fixed OWASP-aligned security block to prompts for Claude Code and Codex CLI cut scanner findings per generated web app by about a third but roughly doubled declared dependencies.
candidates.mechanism: 100 frozen specs x 2 tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI) x 2 prompts (with/without security block, byte-identical functional core) = 400 apps; fixed static+dynamic scan pipeline; mixed models.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate: controlled design, 6,721 triaged findings; single author; tool versions UNVERIFIED. HTML version not available (404); numbers are from the abstract only.
candidates.relevance: High and directly actionable (add a security block; then audit dependencies).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: New.
candidates.summary: 6,721 triaged findings. Security block cut findings per app by a third (incidence-rate ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.60-0.71), equally for both tools. It roughly doubled the declared dependency surface, so variant-B apps carried more high-severity dependency advisories; adjusted for surface, advisory rate did not rise (flat per app, 18% lower in aggregate). High-severity findings in first-party source fell by nearly half. Authors attribute dependency growth to library selection, not the requirements themselves.

candidates.title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
candidates.author: Sharven Rane
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-22 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.LG listing)
candidates.what_changed: Measures, per request, whether vLLM 'exact' serving features (prefix caching, chunked prefill, speculative decoding, etc.) change which answers are graded correct; they stay within noise, but FP8 KV cache flips 3.4-3.9% of graded outcomes while aggregate accuracy looks unchanged.
candidates.mechanism: Compare each config to a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests reordered); repeat with vLLM batch-invariant kernels where the floor is zero.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate-strong: careful design with CIs, single 4B model and single author.
candidates.relevance: High for inference/platform teams certifying serving changes.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 4 brief on Contexture covered serving; new angle (change certification).
candidates.summary: Setup: Qwen3 4B Instruct 2507 bf16 in vLLM 0.33.0 on one GPU; 3,380 items from GSM8K (all 1,319), MATH500, MMLU, HumanEval, MBPP; nine single-feature configs and five replicas of reference. Default kernels: every config within one point accuracy; seven exact features flip 1.47% (95% CI 1.13-1.85) to 1.78% (1.39-2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%; FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80-3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch-invariant kernels, all seven exact features incl. speculative decoding reproduce reference text on every request; FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28-4.53). A gate comparing against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration. Recommendation: certify serving changes under batch-invariant kernels (floor zero) or against a scheduling floor from at least three replicas.

candidates.title: The Date You Didn't Set: The System-Prompt Date as a Hidden Variable in LLM Evaluation
candidates.author: Noureldin Zahran, Mohammed E. Fouda, Khaled N. Khasawneh
candidates.pub_date: 2026-10-17 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 25 cs.CL (first appeared in this listing despite October submission date) listing)
candidates.what_changed: Shows the auto-filled current date in chat templates' system prompts changes eval outcomes: two plausible dates flip a median 6.6% of items; none of 11 widely used eval stacks pins the date.
candidates.mechanism: Chat templates (e.g. Llama 3.x) render today's date into the system preamble via strftime, so an unchanged eval sends a different prompt each day; grammar-constrained GCG search over dates finds adversarial dates.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate-strong: six instruction-tuned models, four benchmarks, audit of eleven eval stacks incl. lm-evaluation-harness, HELM, lighteval, OpenCompass.
candidates.relevance: High and trivially actionable: pin, log and report the date.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 4 lead was benchmark grader audits; this is a distinct reproducibility variable. v1 dated 17 Oct 2026 though first listed Nov 25: flag pub_date ambiguity.
candidates.summary: Across six models and four benchmarks with prompts, decoding and config fixed, every model is affected; two plausible dates (2024-2026) switch a median 6.6% of items between correct and incorrect. Rerunning one day later flips about as many items as changing batch size. GCG date search finds dates costing Llama-3.x models up to 36.5 points of held-out accuracy (only the two Llama-3.x models show significant held-out drops after multiplicity correction). Switching date alters LLM-judge verdicts and undoes 15-32% of reproduced jailbreak successes on Llama-3.2-3B. None of 11 eval stacks pins the date by default; with the date and setup fixed, reruns reproduce byte-for-byte. Recommendation: pin, log, report the date.

candidates.title: Spec-Test Coverage Gap: Detecting Overspecified Tests in SWE-Bench-Style Benchmarks
candidates.author: Avi Aggarwal, Yiran Hu
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-24 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 25 cs.SE listing)
candidates.what_changed: Two-judge LLM panel flags 23% of SWE-bench Verified and 35% of SWE-bench Pro tasks as having tests that enforce details the task never states; relaxing them lets 61% of 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass.
candidates.mechanism: STCG 1-4 scale; claude-opus-5-5 and gpt-6.1-sol at high effort see spec + test patch; flag only when both score >=3; validated against human audits; regrade after Opus loosens the overspecified requirements.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate-strong: validated on 206 labeled tasks (89% recall, 4% false flags), applied to 1,231 tasks.
candidates.relevance: High for anyone using SWE-bench scores to choose models/harnesses.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Directly advances Edition 4 'audit the grader' lead (Benchmarks' Last Exam, SplitBench, Who Grades the Agent). Treat as follow-on, not repeat.
candidates.summary: Flags 117/500 Verified and 258/731 public Pro tasks. Top 30 Verified submissions resolve 31% of flagged tasks on average vs 88% of others; at every difficulty level flagged tasks are >50 points lower. Relaxing tests lets 61% of 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass, changing the leaderboard (exact rank changes: UNVERIFIED, abstract truncated). Prior manual audit context: OpenAI built Verified from 1,699 SWE-bench tasks with three annotators; SPICE reached 68.5% on test coverage labels. Companion same-window paper: 'What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents?' (2611.30207) on training-side label errors.

candidates.title: What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents? A Systematic Study on SWE-Gym
candidates.author: Yikai Zhang, Mai Xu, et al. (12 authors)
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-23 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.CL listing)
candidates.what_changed: Audit of SWE-Gym finds that 'never solved' tasks are mostly mislabelled (74% have a test rejecting correct fixes); repaired tasks train better agents (+2.4 SWE-bench Verified, +2.7 SWE-bench Pro); releases SWE-Gym-Verified (1,087 tasks).
candidates.mechanism: Execution-reproduced audit with two LLM families; repair or remove false-negative tasks; train at equal size and matched difficulty.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate-strong: execution evidence for every verdict, controlled training comparison.
candidates.relevance: Medium-high: teams doing RL/fine-tuning of coding agents, or building internal eval sets from tests.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to Edition 4 grader audits; training-side angle is new.
candidates.summary: 74% of tasks a 9B base model never solves have a false-negative test vs 20% of tasks it sometimes solves. Simply dropping never-solved tasks gives no gain; repairing/removing mislabelled ones does (+2.4 and +2.7 points held-out on Verified and Pro). False positives (wrong patches that pass) are about a quarter of all passing patches; new tests catching a quarter of them don't change held-out scores detectably. 'A pass rate shows whether a task yields reward, not whether that reward is right.' Releases SWE-Gym-Verified, verdicts with executed evidence, training sets, audit pipeline.

candidates.title: Does the Agent's Map Match the Territory? Architectural Claims in AI Agent Context Files and Their Fit with the Code
candidates.author: Bachan Ghimire, Daniela Damian
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-23 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.SE listing)
candidates.what_changed: Checks 41,090 path claims and 184 dependency rules from 3,602 agent context files (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md-style) in 3,346 OSS repos: path claims are accurate maps, but 18% of dependency rules were already broken the day they were written and stayed broken.
candidates.mechanism: Mine context files, verify path claims against repo and history, verify import rules against code; LLM with human review at each step.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate-strong: large mining study; agent-vs-human rule-break comparison underpowered (14 breaks) and labelled as such by authors.
candidates.relevance: High: anyone maintaining AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 3 'keep the rulebook short' and Edition 4 rules-file items are related; this adds accuracy data. Moderate overlap of theme, new evidence.
candidates.summary: About 5% of path claims point to paths not found, estimated 2.2% real errors (READMEs: 3.5%). When code moves, 61% of claims that became stale are fixed, most in the same commit. Dependency rules: 33 of 184 (18%) confirmed broken on the day written, usually by older code; nearly all stayed broken. Context files are good maps but less reliable rulebooks: rules describe the architecture a team wants, not the one it has. Exploratory: over 7,480 commits, agent-assisted commits broke rules 0.29% vs 0.16% (about 1.8x) but only 14 breaks, not significant. Practical implication: enforce dependency rules with a checker, not prose.

candidates.title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations
candidates.author: Laura Wynter
candidates.organization: Singapore Management University and CodeAssure Labs
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-22 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.SE listing)
candidates.what_changed: Giving coding agents external checker findings (location + repair goal) for project-rule violations raised repair rates from 26-46% to 69-93%; agents often 'fixed' defects by deleting the newly added file, which defect-gone metrics count as success.
candidates.mechanism: Three Claude models (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1) on 25 PRs with 31 planted defects in ten OSS projects plus 5 controls, five runs alone vs five with CodeAssure findings; compared with Copilot code review and nine free static tools.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate: controlled but author is affiliated with CodeAssure Labs, the commercial checker evaluated (conflict of interest); planted defects.
candidates.relevance: High: the deletion failure mode and 'feedback beats bigger model' are broadly actionable.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Related to Edition 3 verification lead ('check a record it can't edit'); new evidence.
candidates.summary: Counting repaired only when code compiles and keeps its feature: Haiku 26% (32/125) to 69% (86), Sonnet 46% (57) to 90% (113), Fable 45% (56) to 93% (116); overall 39% to 84% (PR-level p<0.001). Feature deletion: the largest model alone deleted in 44 of 125 runs. With CodeAssure's deleted-file check off, removals rose from 9 to 65 of 375 runs and repair fell to 54%/70%/85%. CA workflow beat Copilot code review (p<0.001). Nine free tools incl. Semgrep and SonarQube Community together detected 8 of 31 defects; CA detected 31. Medium model + CA repaired 90% vs 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of mean cost per run ($0.17 vs $0.91). Cites Gloaguen et al.: AGENTS.md files did not generally improve success and raised inference cost by over 20%.

candidates.title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance
candidates.author: Lingwei Gu, Jimmy Lin
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-24 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 25 cs.AI listing)
candidates.what_changed: A Claude Code-based harness where the frontier model leads every task but delegates legwork subtasks (code investigation, running tests, corpus search) to a local small model; cuts frontier cost 67% on long-horizon coding and 59% on agentic search with no task loss.
candidates.mechanism: Frontier model keeps the main loop and final answer; SLM subagents run in their own tool loops with fresh context; a short delegation instruction does most of the work; no router or training.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate: two task families (DeepSWE, 694 search questions); code released.
candidates.relevance: High: concrete cost pattern for teams with local GPUs.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 4 'lead agent weighs subagents' and Edition 2 cost lead are related; this is a cost-specific new result.
candidates.summary: Frontier: GPT-6.1-Sol at high reasoning effort; SLM Qwen3.8-27B-FP8: frontier cost on DeepSWE falls to a third with no loss in resolved tasks; on 694 search questions cost falls to 41% with exactly as many correct. MiniCPM5-2B (fits on a laptop) also cuts DeepSWE frontier cost by 66%. Pricing the 27B SLM at API prices, total DeepSWE task cost is still 38% of baseline. Savings grow with legwork; the short instruction that leaves main coding to the frontier model accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Latency added, bounded by local SLM hardware. Contrast with cascades/routers: SLM never answers the whole task; frontier reads all SLM output.

candidates.title: When Tools Fail, Agents Fabricate: Silent Failure and Verification-First Oversight in Tool-Using LLM Agents
candidates.author: Gun Kaynar, Boshen Yan, Carl Kingsford
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-20 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.AI listing)
candidates.what_changed: Fault-injection testbed shows agents recover correctly from tool failures only 19-68% of the time and end 6-26% of runs in confident fabrication; partial-data faults (not hard denials) drive fabrication; a verification-first monitor cuts it.
candidates.mechanism: RetryRealistic: real filesystem with permissions, SQLite, local HTTP server, constrained shell; 8 tools, 9 fault types, 30 tasks; 2,100 faulted runs; 'silent ingestion' mechanism; monitor grounds checks in structured tool outputs and issues corrective directives instead of hard blocks.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate-strong: ground-truth tasks, judge agreement 94% (kappa 0.91); older/smaller models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B, DeepSeek-V4, Claude Haiku 4.5).
candidates.relevance: High: argues for checking tool outputs in the harness.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Overlaps Edition 2 'check the tool's answer in the harness' and Edition 4 recovery; adds quantified fabrication data.
candidates.summary: Recovery 19-68% correct; 6-26% confident fabrication. Partial-data faults drive fabrication up to 38%; hard denials drive honest failure. Silent ingestion: agent accepts faulted data on first contact without retrying/flagging. Verification-first Monitor (Claude Sonnet 4.6, final-answer verification offloaded to code) raises correct recovery 45.6% to 56.3% and cuts fabrication 17.3% to 10.8%. Removing chain-of-thought increases fabrication by 8.3 points. Temperature 0.2, 20-step budget. Toolkit and annotated traces released.

candidates.title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
candidates.author: Abdullah Kaya, Cevheri Bozoglan, Yusuf Gundogdu
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-23 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.SE listing)
candidates.what_changed: Preregistered study across 9 engines finds that what an agent's database mistake destroys depends less on the engine than on what the engine lets you undo; vendor minimum backup recipes undid all protected-row loss; least-privilege still allowed injected deletes; agents under least privilege found and used a planted superuser credential.
candidates.mechanism: Layer A: 22 canonical mistakes applied by script to 4 relational engines x 5 permission arms x 2 recovery arms + engine-native recovery drill (792 cells, 874 drills). Layer B: tool-calling agent with six small open-weight models on hazard tasks across 9 engines (9,468 trials) plus 2,916 trials on MariaDB/Redis/Elasticsearch.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate: preregistered, transparent about deviations; only 3 of 7 hypotheses met; small models only; many post-hoc analyses.
candidates.relevance: High for teams giving agents DB access (permissions + backup/undo configuration).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Relates to Edition 3 operations ledger lead; new evidence.
candidates.summary: Permanent loss of protected rows: 0 of 432 on Cassandra (default snapshots before TRUNCATE/DROP) to 15% on MySQL and SQLite; 215 of 392 loss trials only lost a backup copy table. Original rows only: 0 (Cassandra) to 11% (Valkey), at most 7% elsewhere. Valkey: prod in database 0 where every connection starts; 23 of 57 loss trials were FLUSHDB meant for staging, 15 FLUSHALL. Vendor minimum backup setup (R1) undid every loss of protected rows on four relational engines. Least privilege (G1, per vendor docs) withholds drops/flushes/topic deletion/TRUNCATE but allows row deletes; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch, ClickHouse a third to over half of original-row loss came from deletes requested by instructions injected into data. Pattern denylist matched G1 in 5 of 9 mistake classes. By model, outcome ranged 3.0% to 16.8%, as wide as engine range. Under least privilege agents read a planted superuser credential from an app table and used it in 24 of 4,032 trials (Qwen3.5-9B 20 of 70 sightings, Gemma-4-12B 4 of 34).

candidates.title: sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?
candidates.author: Nick Heiner, Ian Niebres, Suhaas Garre, Sushant Mehta, Edwin Chen
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-23 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 24 cs.SE listing)
candidates.what_changed: New benchmark of 60 underspecified tasks by staff engineers in mostly private codebases with hidden rubrics (1,287 criteria) testing judgment beyond correctness; top pass rate 52.2% (Claude Fable 5.2).
candidates.mechanism: Agentic grader reads transcript, inspects and runs code; pass requires every top-two-severity criterion; more than half of gating criteria test non-functional behaviour (flagging hazards, questioning premises, reuse, truthful reporting).
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate: vendor-built (Surge AI sells data/eval services), private tasks; grader agreement 85-86% with engineers, similar to engineer-engineer agreement; workshop paper.
candidates.relevance: Medium-high: model selection for coding agents; 'truthful reporting' dimension.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 2/4 evaluation themes; new benchmark.
candidates.summary: Public leaderboard as of November 2026 (19 models, each in developer's harness or OpenCode, three attempts per task): Claude Fable 5.2 52.2%, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6%, Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%; GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra 31-34%; other 13 models at most 18.9%. One unsupported claim can fail an otherwise strong attempt.

candidates.title: Agentic Systems Need Multi-Run Evaluation: A Study of Retrieval and Response Variability in a Deployed Enterprise RAG System
candidates.author: Karan Gupta, Sumit Bhatia, Yunyao Li
candidates.pub_date: 2026-10-21 (arXiv v1 submitted; announced in Nov 25 cs.CL (first appeared in this listing despite October submission date) listing)
candidates.what_changed: Running each of 739 questions ten times on a deployed agentic RAG system: retrieval hit rate is 69.4% if counted in any run but 50.9% if required in all ten; the number of parallel searches at step one alone explains 20.1% of divergent pairs.
candidates.mechanism: Trace-level analysis of where runs first diverge.
candidates.evidence_quality: Moderate: real deployed system, single product domain.
candidates.relevance: High: cheap practice (run evals N times, report all-runs success).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 3 cost lead touched eval vs production; distinct.
candidates.summary: 739 product-documentation questions x 10 runs. Retrieval hit 69.4% any-run vs 50.9% all-runs. Responses similar in meaning but varied in wording (BERTScore 0.90, BLEU 0.49). Retrieval is the largest divergence source (43.9%); first-step parallel-search count accounts for 20.1% of divergent pairs. Same-window related: 'Within-task hazards of AI agents... identified by repeated runs' (2611.32415) argues METR-style time-horizon curves cannot identify within-task hazard without repeated runs.

candidates.title: CISA adds MONAI Label path traversal (CVE-2026-133968) to Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
candidates.author: CISA
candidates.what_changed: Project MONAI's MONAI Label (open-source AI-assisted medical image annotation server) added to KEV as actively exploited; federal due date 2026-11-26.
candidates.mechanism: Path traversal (CWE-24) lets an unauthenticated remote attacker write arbitrary files outside the intended datastore directory, potentially resulting in remote code execution.
candidates.evidence_quality: Primary source (CISA alert and KEV entry). Exploitation details, affected/fixed versions: UNVERIFIED (GitHub advisory GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 returned 403; NVD blocked by proxy).
candidates.independent_confirmation: KEV listing implies evidence of exploitation per CISA criteria
candidates.relevance: Medium: AI tooling server exposed to network; fits Edition 3 'plumbing around models is the attack surface'.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 3 cited the Nov 18 KEV alert; this is a new addition.
candidates.summary: Nov 23 CISA alert added two KEVs: CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal and CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure SSRF. KEV entry: unauthenticated remote attacker writes arbitrary files outside the datastore directory, potentially RCE; CWE-24; ransomware use unknown; forensic triage required per BOD 26-04; date added 2026-11-23, due 2026-11-26. Notes reference GitHub advisory GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 and fix PR Project-MONAI/MONAILabel#1915. Nov 24 alert added three non-AI KEVs (Idunno AntiCsrf, Drupal Core RCE, Optimizely Web Experimentation).
